terms.definition: A broad design/practice label for moment-to-moment qualities of interaction such as responsiveness, physicality, clarity, impact, amplification and ease/support. It is not admitted as one measurable Game state.
Whether a relevant GameAction can currently be attempted/admitted under current state, mapping, authority and constraints.
The context-bound transformation from control expression into Game-relevant control variables, including gain, acceleration, deadzone, smoothing, filtering, buffering and assistance.
Delay from admitted control/input evidence to authoritative GameAction/control-state effect at the relevant ControlLocus.
Delay from GameAction execution/control change to the authoritative world/task outcome it causes.
Delay from the authoritative event/state/outcome to a feedback signal/representation made available to the participant.
Trial-to-trial or within-stream variation in temporal coupling. Mean latency and jitter are independent dimensions.
Stability/forecastability of action, consequence and feedback timing conditional on context. A fixed nonzero delay can be more predictable than lower but highly variable delay.
Whether feedback is conditionally tied to the authoritative action/state/outcome it purports to represent rather than being false, stale or unrelated.
How reliably the feedback representation exposes the Game-relevant distinction intended to be communicated to the participant, conditional on perceptual access.
Multiple representations/modalities encode an already available Game-relevant distinction. Redundancy may improve robustness/clarity or create clutter depending on implementation/context.
Increasing the magnitude, multiplicity or salience of action/outcome feedback beyond the minimum needed to encode the underlying event. Includes many forms of 'juice'.
Temporal/semantic/spatial agreement among visual, audio, haptic and other feedback cues about one event/action/outcome.

An event-linked presentation intervention such as screen shake, particles, hit flash, audio transient, haptic pulse or camera impulse that amplifies perceived consequence while not necessarily changing authoritative world state.
State-transition dynamics such as acceleration, inertia, gravity, friction, recoil, knockback and recovery that determine actual controlled/world behavior.

Mechanisms such as input buffering, coyote time, command queueing or contextual assistance that preserve/interpret participant intent across timing/state boundaries without necessarily reducing physical/system latency.
Measured ability of the participant/controller or joint controller to produce intended/relevant Game state distinctions under a declared task/evaluation scope.
Human judgment that the system responds promptly/appropriately to control. It can be influenced by timing, predictability, feedback and expectation and is not a raw latency measure.
Human experience/judgment of causing or controlling actions/outcomes. Objective control and action-feedback cues can affect it but are not identical to it.

Human appraisal that an action/outcome has impact, force, weight or punch. It can consume world dynamics and audiovisual/haptic amplification but is not identical to any single cue or physical impulse.
A family of visual/auditory/other embellishment interventions that amplify or redundantly communicate action/outcome events; empirical effects depend on amount, form, success contingency and context.
Human positive/aroused response to an event or feedback treatment. It may mediate or covary with agency/impact judgments but is not Game structural truth.

laws: FeedbackAmplification can change Human agency/impact judgments without changing authoritative GameAction/outcome semantics
PredictableDelay != JitteryDelay even at equal mean latency
SenseOfAgency evidence cannot be used as proof of objective control without independent control evidence

boundaryCases.pressure: Very low latency with weak dynamics/feedback can be objectively responsive without strong impact/weight or positive PlayerValue.
Intentional local temporal pause can increase impact presentation while adding delay; low latency cannot define all good feel.
Nonzero but predictable delay differs from variable/jittery coupling at the same or lower mean latency.
Lower mean latency with high jitter can be less temporally learnable than a stable higher delay.
Strong audiovisual feedback can be intense and prompt yet semantically false, threatening legibility/agency/trust.
Human agency/exhilaration can change while authoritative damage/action semantics remain held fixed.
More amplification can reduce performance/experience; juiciness is not monotonic value.
One modality can provide legible feedback without high visual juice.
More modalities do not guarantee coherence when timing/meaning disagree.
Intent can be supported across action-state windows without reducing device/system latency.
A Game may intentionally admit an action slightly after a physical-state boundary to support intended action semantics.
Weight may arise from authoritative inertia/acceleration dynamics even with minimal screen shake.
Camera shake/slowdown can imply weight while actual world dynamics remain unchanged.
Prompt acknowledgement and semantic clarity matter, but sub-50ms continuous sensorimotor coupling is not the defining requirement.
Latency sensitivity differs by interaction component; control-response demand is action-class dependent.
Small latency changes can affect precision/performance/QoE in latency-sensitive FPS tasks.
Objective performance and subjective agency can move differently under assistance; feel must retain attribution target.
A synthetic policy can have excellent objective control with no Human game-feel evidence.

externalAnchors.pressure: Latency effects depend on interaction class in RTS, supporting action-class-specific timing sensitivity rather than one universal latency threshold.
Controlled CS:GO user study reports degradation in accuracy, score and QoE from added network latency, with weapon/task dependence.

externalAnchors.reference: ACM IMX 2023 Small Latency Variations Do Not Affect Player Performance in First-Person Shooters
externalAnchors.pressure: High base latency reduced performance/experience while small jitter manipulation did not produce the same effect in that experiment; latency dimensions must be measured separately.
Continuous-action assistance/delay study separates objective performance and subjective agency; assisted control can improve both under some delay conditions without exact command execution.
Manipulated feedback validity and action-outcome congruence changed self-agency judgments, showing feedback semantics/context can alter agency inference.
N=3018 action-RPG experiment found both no and extreme juiciness worse than medium/high on multiple performance/experience measures; more juice is not monotonic benefit.
Controlled visual-embellishment studies show visual appeal benefits but limited/context-specific competence effects; juice is not one universal player-experience treatment.

Two custom-game experiments report screen-shake intensity altered reported agency and exhilaration while underlying action/outcome semantics were controlled; visual feedback can retrospectively modulate Human agency judgments.
During new mapping learning, agency judgments shift from temporal contiguity toward learned action-outcome structural correspondence, supporting predictability/learned mapping beyond raw delay alone.

foundationReopen.reason: A decomposes Game Feel into timing, mapping, feedback representation, world dynamics and Human evidence targets already expressible through frozen action/control and owner boundaries; no new primitive is required.
